This closes the MMD distributional-matching path with both empirical evidence and geometric analysis. **Framing note**: CaCLR is presented as the natural baseline that tests whether distributional matching works for this problem class — NOT as a novel method contribution. Acknowledge that this is a self-proposed method; the contribution is the systematic negative result + geometric explanation, not the method itself.\\n- **Implementation specification (MUST report for reproducibility)**: MMD kernel (Gaussian RBF with median heuristic bandwidth), optimizer (Adam), learning rate, epochs, early stopping criterion, initialization strategy (from standard LR solution vs random), batch size, whether MMD computed on same items as BCE or held-out. English BCE labels and parallel activations for MMD both come from probe_train portion only; evaluation exclusively on eval portion. Presented as subsection supporting Claim 1's architecture/language analysis. Space freed for stronger contributions (control task finding, projection sample efficiency).\\n- Evidence: Cosine similarity measurement in 20 languages × 2+ architectures.\\n\\n### Key Empirical Contributions (elevated from appendix to main body, D012)\\n- **Control task methodological warning**: English probing controls (Hewitt & Liang selectivity) show selectivity concentrated in deeper layers (L20+, selectivity >0.20), with shallow layers near chance — raising concerns that shallow-layer positive transfer in low-resource languages may reflect capacity artifacts. Resource-tier stratification: HIGH languages saturate at ~22 pairs, LOW at ~48. Directly actionable for practitioners.\\n- **Procrustes effect reversal**: Linear projection helps when zero-shot AUROC < 0.50 but hurts when > 0.60. Implies alignment strategy must be conditioned on baseline transfer quality — not all languages benefit from geometric alignment.\\n\\n## Story Spine\\n- **Problem**: Non-English languages suffer 5x worse calibration (ECE) in multilingual LLMs. Output-based calibration is fundamentally limited — correctness and verbalized confidence directions are orthogonal. Existing fixes require per-language data (LACE) or 5x inference cost (MKA).\\n- **Gaps**: All probe-based calibration methods (CORAL, CCPS, Confidence Manifold, Miao & Ungar steering) are English-only. Nobody has tested whether this research line works multilingually. Xiao et al. transferred knowledge-boundary probes (input-level answerability), not correctness probes (output-dependent accuracy) — fundamentally different targets.\\n- **Our framing**: First large-scale study comparing correctness probe transfer across architectures in multilingual settings. Core novel findings: (1) Simpson's Paradox in CKA-transfer relationship — raw correlation negative (depth confound), partial correlation positive (within-layer, higher CKA = better transfer) — a genuine geometric insight not predicted by prior work; (2) English probing controls reveal layer-dependent selectivity, suggesting shallow-layer low-resource results may be capacity artifacts (control task warning for the field; cross-lingual quantification pending); (3) linear projection with ~50 pairs is the practical solution, with resource-tier-dependent saturation. We discover the local Pareto tradeoff at the deepest layers (overall depth-transfer trend is positive), decompose transfer into difficulty/capability components, test CaCLR as the natural distributional-matching baseline, and provide CKA geometric analysis of why transfer succeeds or fails. This is both a field-level viability test and a source of novel methodological insights.\\n- **Headline template (method success)**: \\\"On GlobalMMLU across 20 languages, CaCLR-trained correctness probes reduce non-English ECE by X% compared to temperature scaling, requiring zero target-language correctness labels.\\\"\\n- **Headline template (negative result)**: \\\"Cross-lingual correctness probe transfer reveals architecture-dependent depth effects; the natural distributional-matching approach (CaCLR) fails, but simple linear projection with ~50 parallel pairs is the most effective label-free transfer method.\\\" Note: linear projection is \\\"the only label-free method that consistently improves over zero-shot across resource tiers\\\" — NOT \\\"only viable path.\\\" Zero-shot is viable for high-resource (AUROC>0.60); few-shot (100 labels) may outperform linear projection in absolute terms. CaCLR outcome pending. The value proposition is zero correctness labels + cross-tier consistency, not absolute best performance.\\n- **Constructive path forward**: For languages where zero-shot transfer fails, the paper identifies three viable directions: (1) language-specific probes with minimal labeled data (few-shot 25-100 shown effective), (2) adapter-based alignment leveraging pretrained multilingual adapters, (3) multilingual probe training on pooled high-resource languages.\\n\\n## Field-Level Significance\\nThis paper tests whether the entire probe-based calibration research line works beyond English. Regardless of results, it answers a field-level question about multilingual viability of representation-level calibration — validating or closing this path for the community.\\n\\n## Anticipated Reviewer Concerns & Responses\\n1. **\\\"Xiao et al. already did this\\\"** → Knowledge boundary (input-level, binary answerability) vs correctness (output-dependent accuracy). They measure probing accuracy, not calibration. 8 languages vs our 20+. No Pareto frontier. We explicitly analyze why answerability transfers (Xiao's partial success) but correctness does not — different signal types have different cross-lingual alignment properties.\\n2. **\\\"Temperature scaling baseline\\\"** → We compare against it. CaCLR optimizes during training, not post-hoc. Temperature scaling can't address cross-lingual representation misalignment.\\n3. **\\\"Mean-shift too weak / why does it fail?\\\"** → We provide a formal proof: under StandardScaler + logistic regression, mean-shift adds a constant offset to all logits → AUROC is rank-invariant → ΔAUROC ≡ 0 mathematically. MVP data confirms: ΔAUROC = 0.000000 across all 5 languages × all layers. ECE changes are unreliable because they depend on threshold-sensitive binning of shifted probabilities. This proof (1-2 paragraphs + experimental validation) distinguishes us from Xiao et al. (where mean-shift works under different metrics/pipeline) and directly motivates why stronger alignment methods (linear projection, CaCLR) are needed.\\n4. **\\\"Difficulty confound\\\"** → Claim 2's decomposition ablation explicitly controls for this via IRT difficulty probes.\\n5. **\\\"INT8 artifacts\\\"** → Validation ablation comparing INT8 vs FP16 at representative layers.\\n6. **\\\"Only MCQA\\\"** → Acknowledged. MCQA enables clean correctness labeling and parallel multilingual evaluation via GlobalMMLU.\\n7. **\\\"Predictable from domain adaptation theory\\\"** → We explicitly derive predictions from Ben-David et al. (2010) H-divergence framework and test them. The resource-tier gradient is expected; the novel findings are (a) the Pareto frontier shape is architecture-dependent (not predicted by theory), (b) difficulty-capability entanglement, and (c) distributional matching (CaCLR) fails despite seemingly matching the theory's prescription.\\n8. **\\\"No statistical tests\\\"** → All key comparisons include bootstrap CIs (1000 resamples) and paired permutation tests across languages. Effect sizes reported with Cohen's d.\\n9. **\\\"Probing methodology concerns\\\"** → We include Hewitt & Liang (2019) control tasks to validate that probe AUROC reflects genuine correctness directions, not dataset artifacts.\\n10. **\\\"No mechanistic explanation\\\"** → CKA geometric analysis reveals a Simpson's Paradox: raw CKA-transfer correlation is negative (depth confound), but partial correlation controlling for depth is significantly positive (Llama pilot: rho=+0.41, p=0.006; 14/17 layer-level correlations positive). Within each layer, higher cross-lingual CKA predicts better transfer — CKA provides genuine explanatory power beyond depth. Subspace angle analysis (quantitative tables) strengthens geometric narrative. Frame as \\\"geometric analysis\\\" not \\\"mechanistic explanation.\\\" **Transparency requirements**: (a) Report Qwen pilot non-significant (rho=+0.18, p=0.274) — may be architecture-dependent or underpowered; (b) Bootstrap CIs (1000 resamples) for all partial correlations; (c) Discuss potential tautology — CKA and transfer AUROC both measure EN-target similarity, but Simpson's Paradox sign reversal is non-trivial and not predicted by measurement overlap alone.\\n11. **\\\"Why not conformal prediction?\\\"** → Discussed in Related Work. Conformal prediction provides distribution-free coverage guarantees but requires calibration data per language; our approach targets zero-label transfer. Complementary, not competing.\\n12. **\\\"CaCLR parallel activations = test leakage?\\\"** → Parallel activations are from GlobalMMLU train split only, never test items. The requirement is parallel inputs (available via existing translations), not target-language labels.\\n13. **\\\"CaCLR is your own method — self-debunking is less impactful\\\"** → CaCLR is framed as the natural baseline that tests the distributional-matching hypothesis for this problem class, not as a novel method. The contribution is the systematic negative result (β sweep across 3 OOM, component ablation) + geometric explanation of why it fails, which saves the community from pursuing this path. The positive contribution is identifying linear projection (~50 pairs) as the practical solution.\\n14. **\\\"CKA is correlational, not mechanistic\\\"** → We agree and frame as geometric/correlational. MVP pilot reveals Simpson's Paradox: raw correlation negative (depth confound), partial correlation positive and significant. CKA adds genuine explanatory power beyond depth. Full-scale analysis (20 languages) with bootstrap CIs will confirm. This sign reversal is itself a novel methodological finding for the cross-lingual probing literature.\\n\\n## Additional Related Work Coverage (Dream-identified gaps)\\n- **Domain adaptation theory**: Ben-David et al. (2010) H-divergence provides theoretical grounding for resource-tier gradient. Zhao et al. (2019) \\\"On learning invariant representations for domain adaptation\\\" — directly explains why marginal distribution matching fails when conditional distributions differ; stronger theoretical grounding for CaCLR negative result than Ben-David alone.\\n- **Cross-lingual alignment**: MUSE (Conneau et al. 2018), VecMap (Artetxe et al. 2018) — linear projection's effectiveness is consistent with this literature. Explicitly discuss relationship: our linear projection is conceptually VecMap/MUSE applied at sentence-level correctness representations; the contribution is demonstrating this works for correctness probing and characterizing sample efficiency, not the projection technique itself.\\n- **Representation similarity**: CKA (Kornblith et al. 2019), SVCCA (Raghu et al. 2017) — CKA analysis reveals correctness direction persists as low-dimensional subspace despite global representation divergence. Must report partial correlation controlling for depth.\\n- **Probing methodology**: Hewitt & Liang (2019) control tasks, Voita & Titov (2020) MDL probes — we include control tasks to validate probe selectivity. Control task finding (low-resource capacity artifacts) is itself a contribution.\\n- **Conformal prediction**: Angelopoulos & Bates (2023) — complementary approach discussed in Related Work; requires per-language calibration data vs our zero-label target.\\n- **Cross-lingual transfer learning**: Pires et al. (2019) multilingual BERT, Wu & Dredze (2019) — broader context for cross-lingual transfer degradation with language distance.\\n- **DALI**: Ravisankar et al. (2026) — cross-lingual representation alignment; must cite if published.\\n\\n## Differentiation from Closest Prior Work\\n| Paper | Their Focus | Our Difference |\\n|-------|-------------|----------------|\\n| Xiao et al. (ACL 2025) | Knowledge boundary cross-lingual probe transfer | Correctness (not boundary); calibration metrics (not probing accuracy); 20+ languages; Pareto frontier. We analyze WHY answerability transfers but correctness does not. |\\n| LACE (Zhou et al.) | Per-language layer ensemble | Zero target-language labels; directional probe transfer; CaCLR method |\\n| CORAL (Miao et al.) | Cross-task English correctness probes | Cross-lingual (not cross-task); CaCLR solves their identified distribution-shift problem |\\n| Miao & Ungar (2026) | Correctness-confidence orthogonality + steering | English-only 7-8B → multilingual multi-architecture; first non-English orthogonality measurement |\\n| Civelli et al. | Cross-lingual difficulty probe transfer | Correctness (not difficulty); difficulty is their control for our ablation |\\n\", \"total_chars\": 19187, \"truncated\": false}, \"error\": null, \"metadata\": {}}"}

2	\label{sec:intro}
3	
4	Multilingual deployment of large language models (LLMs) exposes a critical calibration gap: non-English users receive substantially worse confidence estimates, with Expected Calibration Error (ECE) up to 5$\times$ higher in low-resource languages \cite{zhou2025lace}. Standard post-hoc methods such as temperature scaling \cite{guo2017calibration} require per-language validation data, and verbalized confidence \cite{kadavath2022language} operates on output logits without accessing internal representations. A recent line of work identifies an alternative signal: LLM hidden states encode a ``correctness direction'' nearly orthogonal to verbalized confidence (cosine similarity below 0.04) \cite{miao2026closing}, and correctness probes trained on this direction achieve approximately 50\% ECE improvement over output-based baselines \cite{miao2026coral}. Both CCPS \cite{khanmohammadi2025ccps} and the Confidence Manifold framework \cite{confidence_manifold2026} confirm that calibration-relevant information concentrates in low-dimensional representational subspaces. All of these probe-based calibration methods, however, have been developed and evaluated exclusively in English.
5	
6	No prior work has tested whether correctness probes transfer across languages. The closest studies address related but distinct targets. \citet{xiao2025knowledge} probe knowledge boundaries (an input-level property of whether a question is answerable), not correctness (an output-dependent property of whether the model answered correctly). \citet{civelli2026shared} probe item difficulty using Item Response Theory (IRT) labels, a language-agnostic question property independent of any particular model's response. Neither study reports calibration metrics (ECE, Brier score) or compares multiple transfer strategies. DALI \cite{ravisankar2026dali} provides causal evidence through activation patching that English middle-layer representations can repair errors in 24 non-English languages, which confirms that transferable correctness information exists but does not quantify when or why probe-level transfer fails. This gap motivates three research questions: (1) Does the correctness direction persist across languages, or is it language-specific? (2) How does cross-lingual transfer depend on representation geometry, specifically layer depth and cross-lingual representational similarity? (3) Can distributional matching shift the transfer frontier without target-language correctness labels?
7	
8	We present the first large-scale study of correctness probe transfer across architectures. The shape of this Pareto frontier varies across architectures: Qwen exhibits a strong monotonic tradeoff, while Llama displays language-specific patterns.
9	
10	This tradeoff conceals a deeper geometric structure. \section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

Multilingual deployment of large language models (LLMs) exposes a critical calibration gap: non-English users receive substantially worse confidence estimates, with Expected Calibration Error (ECE) up to 5$\times$ higher in low-resource languages \cite{zhou2025lace}. Standard post-hoc methods such as temperature scaling \cite{guo2017calibration} require per-language validation data, and verbalized confidence \cite{kadavath2022language} operates on output logits without accessing internal representations. A recent line of work identifies an alternative signal: LLM hidden states encode a ``correctness direction'' nearly orthogonal to verbalized confidence (cosine similarity below 0.04) \cite{miao2026closing}, and correctness probes trained on this direction achieve approximately 50\% ECE improvement over output-based baselines \cite{miao2026coral}. Both CCPS \cite{khanmohammadi2025ccps} and the Confidence Manifold framework \cite{confidence_manifold2026} confirm that calibration-relevant information concentrates in low-dimensional representational subspaces. All of these probe-based calibration methods, however, have been developed and evaluated exclusively in English.

No prior work has tested whether correctness probes transfer across languages. The closest studies address related but distinct targets. \citet{xiao2025knowledge} probe knowledge boundaries (an input-level property of whether a question is answerable), not correctness (an output-dependent property of whether the model answered correctly). \citet{civelli2026shared} probe item difficulty using Item Response Theory (IRT) labels, a language-agnostic question property independent of any particular model's response. Neither study reports calibration metrics (ECE, Brier score) or compares multiple transfer strategies. DALI \cite{ravisankar2026dali} provides causal evidence through activation patching that English middle-layer representations can repair errors in 24 non-English languages, which confirms that transferable correctness information exists but does not quantify when or why probe-level transfer fails. This gap motivates three research questions: (1) Does the correctness direction persist across languages, or is it language-specific? (2) How does cross-lingual transfer depend on representation geometry, specifically layer depth and cross-lingual representational similarity? (3) Can distributional matching shift the transfer frontier without target-language correctness labels?

We present the first large-scale study of correctness probe transfer across architectures. The study covers 2+ model families, 20 languages in three resource tiers, and 5 transfer methods evaluated on GlobalMMLU. In 7B-scale pilot experiments, we observe an architecture-dependent depth-transferability tradeoff (Figure~\ref{fig:pareto}): deeper layers yield better English probe quality but degrade cross-lingual transfer. The shape of this Pareto frontier varies across architectures: Qwen exhibits a strong monotonic tradeoff, while Llama displays language-specific patterns.

The raw correlation between Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA) \cite{kornblith2019cka} and transfer Area Under the ROC Curve (AUROC) across all language-layer pairs is negative, because both quantities covary with depth. After controlling for depth via partial correlation, the sign reverses: within each layer, higher cross-lingual CKA predicts better probe transfer. In 7B-scale pilot analysis, this partial correlation is significant for Llama-3.1-8B ($\rho = +0.41$, $p = 0.006$); Qwen2.5-7B shows a consistent but underpowered trend ($\rho = +0.18$, $p = 0.274$, $n=40$). Full-scale validation across 20 languages (\S\ref{sec:geometric}) will determine generality. This Simpson's Paradox exposes a confounding pattern that naive cross-layer pooling obscures: what appears as a negative CKA-transfer association in aggregate is in fact a positive within-layer relationship.

We also design Calibration-aware Cross-Lingual Regularization (CaCLR), a distributional matching objective ($\mathcal{L}_{\text{BCE}} + \alpha \cdot \mathcal{L}_{\text{SB-ECE}} + \beta \cdot \mathcal{L}_{\text{consistency}}$), as a principled test of whether Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) alignment can improve zero-correctness-label transfer (results pending experimental validation).

Our experimental framework provides systematic coverage along four axes, with full-scale replication on frontier-scale models. We test 2+ architectures (Qwen3-235B-A22B and Llama 4 Scout 17B-16E as primary models) across 20 languages that span high, medium, and low resource tiers. We compare 5 transfer methods ordered by complexity: zero-shot application, mean-shift alignment, Procrustes rotation, few-shot probe retraining, and CaCLR (\S\ref{sec:transfer}). All transfer methods except few-shot retraining satisfy a zero-correctness-label constraint and need no target-language correctness annotations. We decompose probe targets into difficulty-shared and capability-specific components through IRT-based projection (\S\ref{sec:decomposition}), which explains why transfer succeeds at some layers and fails at others. CKA geometric analysis with depth-controlled partial correlation provides the diagnostic framework to explain failure modes (\S\ref{sec:geometric}).

Our contributions are:
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Architecture-dependent Pareto frontier and CKA geometric analysis.} We discover that cross-lingual correctness probe transfer exhibits a depth-transferability tradeoff whose shape varies across architectures. A Simpson's Paradox in the CKA-transfer relationship reveals that within-layer representational similarity predicts transfer success, a confounding pattern obscured by naive cross-layer pooling (\S\ref{sec:geometric}).

\item \textbf{Difficulty-capability decomposition.} We decompose cross-lingual transfer into a difficulty-shared component (transferable at all depths) and a capability-specific component (responsible for deep-layer degradation), which yields prescriptive predictions for alignment strategy selection (\S\ref{sec:decomposition}; experiments in progress).

\item \textbf{CaCLR distributional matching test.} We design CaCLR ($\mathcal{L}_{\text{BCE}} + \alpha \cdot \mathcal{L}_{\text{SB-ECE}} + \beta \cdot \mathcal{L}_{\text{consistency}}$) as a principled baseline that tests whether MMD-based distributional matching can improve zero-correctness-label transfer. Results are pending experimental validation (\S\ref{sec:transfer}).

\item \textbf{Empirical contributions with practical implications.} (a) Control task analysis reveals that probe selectivity concentrates in deeper layers, raising concerns about capacity artifacts in low-resource shallow-layer transfer, a field-level methodological warning (\S\ref{sec:controls}). (b) Linear projection with approximately 50 parallel pairs achieves near-optimal transfer with resource-tier-dependent saturation. ## 一、总体写作哲学

### 1.1 故事驱动，不是数据堆砌

- 论文必须以"故事线"为核心展开：问题 → 洞察 → 方法 → 验证

### 1.3 专有名词必须有定义

### 2.1 四个必答问题（150-250 words）

Abstract 必须在很短的篇幅内清楚回答：

# Cross-Lingual Calibration — Writing Patterns (8 papers)

## Narrative

**Story type**: "突破局限型" (7/8). Blind spot → reveal → fill. High conf.

**Intro**: 4 paragraphs (5/8). P1 motivation → P2 prior work → P3 gap+approach → P4 three contributions [(1) discovery, (2) method, (3) generalization]. High conf.

**Hooks** (pick one):
- English-centric gap: "Prior work focuses on English, leaving X unexplored" (xiao, zhou). 2/8.
- Name the meta-problem: "Square One Bias" (zhou) — forces acknowledgment.
- Cognitive dissonance: "LLMs are surprisingly well-calibrated" (joshi) — contradicts expectation.
- Pain narrowing: "most dangerous hallucination — confident wrong answers" (ji).

**Tension**: Show standard practice actively fails, not just untried. "Fine-tuning doesn't change alignment" (liu). "Final layer overwrites multilingual signals" (zhou). "Aggregate correlation masks instance-level failure" (ravisankar). 3/8. High conf.

## Insight Delivery

**Layer-wise revelation** (3/8): Probe all layers → phase transition → motivates method. Signature move of this subfield.

**Negative-as-evidence** (2/8): "X doesn't work" proves your design. SAE failure → distributed signal → justifies probe (miao2026coral). SFT doesn't align → explicit alignment needed (liu).

**"Finding the knob"** (ji): Abstract concept → manipulable direction. Provides understanding + intervention.

## Figures

**Figure 1**: 50/50 motivation (analytical) vs method overview (method papers). High conf.

**Layer analysis → line plots** (universal). Overlay conditions on same axes. Never tables for continuous layer data. High conf.

**Xling transfer → heatmaps**. Side-by-side at contrasting layers (xiao: layer 3 vs 19). 3/8.

**Gain highlighting**: Dashed baseline line (miao2026coral), before/after panels (xiao), curve gaps (ji). 4/8.

**Progression**: motivation → method → finding → ablation → surprise. 14+ figures: front-load key results, appendix for per-language. 6/8.

## Tables

**Main result**: rows=methods, cols=datasets×metrics, grouped by dataset. Bold best. 3-4 baselines main, full in appendix. 5/8. High conf.

**Ablations**: full numbers (8/8). No checkmark grids. Delta-from-base rare. High conf.

**Division**: Continuous → figures. Discrete comparisons → tables. Per-language → appendix. Mechanistic = figure-heavy; benchmarking = table-heavy. High conf.

**Appendix**: Main 1-2 models + key langs. Appendix exhaustive. zhou: 15 main, 122 appendix. 6/8.
